title: Divorce (Gittin 90b)
hook: divorce needs a written document; the Talmud says the altar weeps, yet it is permitted

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ketubah, the marriage contract the wife keeps. Your line was protection in writing. Did you put one promise into writing? Today, the end of the week, and a harder page. Day one thousand seventy-eight.

Some readers say the last page of a tractate is where the rabbis leave something they want remembered. Tractate Gittin, the book of divorce, spends page after page on the technical details: who writes the document, who signs it, how it's delivered. Then, on its final page, the Mishnah records an argument about when a man may divorce his wife, and the Talmud adds a single sentence. Divorce is permitted. And yet when a man divorces the wife of his youth, even the altar sheds tears. Today: a law that allows something and grieves it at the same time.
screen: `PAGE AFTER PAGE OF DETAILS.` → `THE LAST PAGE.` → `EVEN THE ALTAR SHEDS TEARS.`

segments.voice: Get. A get is the Jewish document of divorce. First, it has to be written. The Torah describes a man who, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "writeth her a bill of divorcement, and giveth it in her hand." Not a word spoken in anger, not a door slammed. A written document, carefully made, delivered into her hand. The care slows things down, and it gives her proof that she is free. Second, the argument. The Mishnah records three views about the grounds. The school of Shammai says only for a serious sexual wrong. The school of Hillel says even if she spoiled his cooking. Rabbi Akiva says even if he found someone more beautiful. The rabbis are arguing, out loud, about how easy it should be to end a marriage, and the law, as later codes follow it, does permit divorce. Third, the tears. Right after this argument, the Talmud quotes a sage who says that whoever divorces his first wife, even the altar sheds tears over him. It draws on the prophet Malachi, who rebukes men who cover the altar with weeping, and calls the abandoned wife "the wife of thy covenant." Notice what that does. The law stays the law. A marriage that cannot go on may end. But the text refuses to pretend that an ending is nothing. Permission and grief, side by side, on the same page. Look back over this week and you'll see that same pairing again and again: the fathers of work and the rest they leave room for, a string that makes a home, joy given a frame, a fast that points to deeds, a contract that guards a wife. Now a document that frees, written next to tears. Even the altar weeps.
screen: `WRITTEN, AND GIVEN IN HER HAND.` · `SHAMMAI, HILLEL, AKIVA.` · `EVEN THE ALTAR SHEDS TEARS.` · `PERMISSION AND GRIEF, SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `EVEN THE ALTAR WEEPS.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: honor one hard ending. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind something that ended. A marriage, a friendship, a job, a home, a version of yourself. Maybe it was right that it ended. Maybe it's still sore. You don't have to decide. Just let both be true for a minute: it was allowed to end, and it's all right to grieve it. If something in you wants to cry for it, let the altar cry with you. The bell holds the time.
Get. The Jewish document of divorce, written with care and given into the wife's hand, permitted, and grieved. Today's word.
Your line: even the altar weeps. Today, when someone tells you about something that ended, don't rush to say it was for the best. Let it be sad first. Day one thousand seventy-eight.

howItsDone: In Orthodox and Conservative communities a get is written by a scribe and given before a rabbinical court, alongside any civil divorce; Reform Judaism generally accepts a civil divorce, and some Reform rabbis offer a ritual of parting.

fork.setup: you're a sage at the end of tractate Gittin. divorce is permitted, and sometimes it has to happen. what do you add?
options: permit it and say nothing more.
permit it, and say even the altar weeps.
fork.reveal: the Talmud does the third: the law stays, and the text says that even the altar sheds tears over a man who divorces his first wife.
